items.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996
items.q: Much as I would like to write some stuff like Duke Ellington or other great arrangers or composers.

ctx.x: Well capturing my voice is really not too hard, because as I discovered on the saxophone, as much as I try to sound like Cannonball and Bird, I sound like Bob. So the thing is to accept who you are. That’s the hardest thing. And once you accept who you are, then it’s really easy because I work with Sam Rivers, and he’s avante garde. And he’s in his 60s

but as he reminds me, when he played bebop, that was avante garde. So he’s always been avante garde. And we were on a train one time over in Europe and we were with this group of tenor saxophones called the Winds of Manhattan. And he said let me show you something. Because I was watching and he’d be writing without no piano. And sometimes he’d cut this page and put it over here, and he’d just be writing, without a score. And he says, I said, “How do you do that?” And he says, “Here, take a bit of paper. Write…

I want to say one other thing is your rhythm section players did a marvelous little workshop with our students this afternoon, and they did something, I want you to make a little comment on this. They were playing and I mean we knew our kids couldn’t keep up with that. But I would make your rhythm section play then I would make one of our students take a solo.
